Title: How to go fractional or build a SaaS · Madgrowth

For leaders in tech and solopreneurs with 5+ years of experience

# From operator to owner.

You have the experience, the network and more ideas than time. Madgrowth helps you pick the one business worth building, turn it into an offer people pay for and land your first clients, with agents you run yourself or 1:1 with me.

Madalena Rugeroni · ex-Google, advisor and investor · scaled startups from 0 to $10M in revenue · runs a portfolio of internet businesses today     Madalena RugeroniFounder of Madgrowth, Mazo and Favorite People

Advising leaders in tech from companies like

Where it stalls

## Most leaders in tech know roughly what they want to build. Then it sits for months.

You've shipped products, led teams and hit targets at companies people know. You want more control over your time and something of your own. Maybe that's a fractional role, an advisory practice, an agency or a SaaS idea you keep coming back to. Four questions keep it from starting.

01

### Is this the right thing to build?

You have an idea, maybe three. With no way to test them against the market and against how you like to work, all of them stay open and none of them start.

02

### Who buys it, and why me?

"I help companies grow" gives nobody a reason to call. A buyer has to recognize their problem in one line and see why you're the person to fix it.

03

### How do I package and price it?

Day rate, retainer, project or product. Most people anchor on their last salary, charge too little and end up with more work than they planned.

04

### Where do the first clients come from?

Your network gets you a few conversations. After that you need people who already know what you do before you pitch them, and that audience takes months to build.

How it works

## Five steps from an idea to paying clients

It's the sequence I used to build my own businesses. Every product below follows these five steps. The difference is who does the work.

01

### Decide
Is this worth building?
The Go / No-Go scores your idea against the market and your Builder Archetype, then gives you the cheapest way to test it. No idea yet? Start with the free Expertise Audit.

02

### Position it
Who buys it, and why me?
Customer interviews, your ICP, positioning and messaging. Every claim gets an evidence grade, so you know what's proven and what's still a guess.

03

### Package it
What do I sell, and for how much?
The offer, the price and the numbers behind it. You end with a clear scope, a price you can defend and a check that the economics work.

04

### Build the audience
Who hears about it?
A content plan built from your messaging and one lead magnet that leads to your offer. Start this early, because inbound takes months to build.

05

### Launch it
Who pays first?
The landing page, the launch plan, your acquisition channels, the sales conversation and a client's first 90 days.

You do the work.   The Build · 1,200€/month We do all five together 1:1 with me for 90 days, with The Stack included.

Who it's for

## For leaders in tech ready to build something of their own

A fractional role, an advisory practice, an agency or a SaaS product all start with the same decisions: what you sell, who buys it and what you charge.

### Still employed, ready for more autonomy

Product, growth, revenue and engineering leaders with 5 to 10+ years at startups and scale-ups. You want flexibility and income that doesn't depend on one employer, and you'd rather build it while you still have the job.

### Recently independent

Fractional executives, consultants, agency founders and solo founders in their first year, including anyone fresh out of a layoff. You have deep expertise and a network. You still need a clear offer, a price and your first three clients.

### Ready to build a product

Operators who want to turn a problem they've dealt with for years into software or a digital product, with evidence people will pay before six months go into building it.

Already running a startup and need help with go-to-market strategy and scaling it? Startup GTM advisory →

Why not just…

## Options you've probably considered

### …ask ChatGPT or Claude?

You'll get generic advice that could fit any business. The Stack runs the agent for the business you're building, whether that's a fractional or advisory practice, a service or a SaaS. Each agent comes from my own go-to-market work and from experts in that specific topic. See the agents →

### …take a creator course?

The catch with courses is finishing them: most people stop partway through the videos. The Stack has you build your audience as you go, with a content plan from your positioning and a lead magnet that leads to your offer. In The Build I review it with you and keep you posting.

### …join a fractional marketplace?

Useful once you know exactly what you sell and to whom. Marketplaces take a cut of every engagement and expect you to pitch yourself.

### …figure it out alone?

Possible. It's also why so many people think about this for a year or more and never launch.

About

## hi, I'm Madalena. I turn tech operators into owners.

Over the last decade, I've lived the tech operator trap.

Leading teams at Google. Scaling startups from zero to $10M in revenue. Six-figure salary, fancy titles, and zero ownership of my time.

I had built everything the agent said to build. But my income still depended on one employer, my expertise was trapped inside someone else's company, and my time wasn't my own.

So I built a way out. Then I built Madgrowth to help others do the same. Today I advise and invest in startups and run a portfolio of internet businesses.

I work with leaders in tech who are done building for others and ready to build for themselves, whether that's a fractional role, a services business or software.

I've been where you are: the knowledge, the experience and the drive, with no clear path to make it work independently.

That's the path I'll help you find.

FAQ

## Questions, answered

Do I need to quit my job?

No. The system is built to run alongside a job, and most clients create their first offer while still employed.

What if I don't know what I'd sell?

Many people have a direction and no specific offer yet. The free Expertise Audit finds your three strongest angles in about ten minutes, using the career you already have, and the Go / No-Go tells you which one is worth building.

I already use ChatGPT or Claude. Why pay for The Stack?

A general assistant gives you a reasonable answer for any business. The Stack runs a specific agent for the business you're building, based on my own go-to-market work and on frameworks from practitioners like April Dunford and Blair Enns. Each agent uses what the earlier ones produced and ends with a document you keep: an ICP, an offer, a price, a launch plan.

Fractional, services or software: does it matter which?

Not at the start. All of them begin with what you sell, who buys it and what it costs. The Stack has a version of each agent for each model, and in The Build we adapt the plan to yours. The Go / No-Go scores the idea against your Builder Archetype before you commit months to it.

I have around 5 years of experience. Is that enough?

If you've owned an outcome, like a number, a team or a launch, yes. The Expertise Audit looks for the angle in the work you've done, whatever your title was.

Do I need a big audience?

Not a big one. You do need a focused one, and it pays to start early. The audience step builds it from a content plan and one lead magnet, and a few hundred of the right people is enough to launch.

How do I go from a tech job to fractional or consulting work?

Start with a problem you've solved more than once and a type of company that has that problem and the budget to fix it. Package it as a monthly retainer with a clear scope and sell it to your network first. The Builder Diagnostic shows whether fractional work suits how you operate, and The Stack takes you through positioning, the offer and pricing.

How should I price a fractional role or consulting offer?

Price against the cost of the problem and the full-time hire the client would otherwise make, and sell a defined monthly scope in place of hours. The Pricing skill in The Stack runs this with Blair Enns and Alan Weiss for services and Madhavan Ramanujam for software.

The Stack, The Read or The Build?

They follow the same five steps. The Stack is the fifteen agents to run on your own (299€ once). The Read is my written review of where you are on each step (599€). The Build is all five steps with me, 1:1 (1,200€/month, 3-month minimum). If you're unsure, book the free 15-minute call from The Build card.

Do I have to run the skills in order?

No. The first agent you run asks eight questions about your business, once. Every other agent reads those answers, so you can start with the Go / No-Go, pricing or the landing page. The recommended sequence starts with Decide, and you're free to skip around.

Can I talk to you before starting The Build?

Yes. Book the 15-minute call from The Build card and bring your diagnostic profile. If you want an in-depth review of your plan, that's The Read.

I'm already running a startup. Where can I get go-to-market help?

This page is for building something new. For a startup that's already running, there are two options.

1:1 with me. I advise founders between 0 and $1M in revenue on go-to-market strategy and scaling. See startup GTM advisory →

Self-serve, for B2B SaaS. Mazo is my AI go-to-market advisor. It reviews your go-to-market using your own numbers, pushes back when it disagrees and sets the tests to run next. Try Mazo →

Title: The Stack: 15 AI agents to decide, position, price and launch · Madgrowth

The Stack · 15 AI agents

# Fifteen AI agents, each with a version for your kind of business.

A SaaS product and a fractional CMO practice need different positioning, pricing and launch methods. The Stack classifies your business first. Every agent then runs the frameworks built for that model and hands you a finished document.

Get the Stack · 299€ → See the fifteen agents ↓    Built by Madalena Rugeroni · ex-Google, advisor and investor · scaled startups from 0 to $10M in revenue

An agent for each model

ServicesSoftwareProductLocalMediaMarketplaces
Free updates. Installs as Claude skills, in the app or Claude Code.

How it works

## Answer the setup questions once. Every agent uses them.

1

### Classify your business

The setup step asks about your model, stage, sales motion, price point, team, Builder Archetype, geography and how much you can build yourself. It takes a few minutes.

2

### Load the agent

Every agent opens the version for your model. A fractional CMO pricing a retainer gets Blair Enns. A SaaS founder gets Madhavan Ramanujam.

3

### Keep the output

Each agent ends with a document: an ICP, an offer, a price, a page spec, a launch calendar. The next one builds on it, so start wherever the pressure is.

ServicesFractional roles, consulting, advisory, agencies
SoftwareB2B SaaS, sales-led or product-led
ProductConsumer and digital products sold online
LocalBusinesses built around a place
MediaNewsletters, podcasts, communities
MarketplacesA layer on top of any model

The agents

## What each agent produces and the frameworks behind it

Frameworks are listed for the models where they apply. They're credited to their authors, who aren't affiliated with Madgrowth.

### Start here

Run these two first. The Expertise Audit is also free on its own.
Free + setup

FreeExpertise Audit
Your three strongest angles from the career you already have, each with who buys, the problem in their words and your proof.

- All modelsDavid C. Baker's test for experts: what you've done repeatedly, what people already come to you for and who has budget for it

SetupStart
A context file every other skill reads, so you answer these questions once.

- CoversBusiness model, stage, sales motion, price band, solo or team, Builder Archetype, geography and build capacity

### Decide

Is this idea worth building, and is it right for you? A verdict before you spend months on it.
Agent 01

01Go / No-Go
A go, no-go or not-yet verdict on your business idea, scored against your Builder Archetype, with the assumption that decides it, the cheapest way to test it and a pre-mortem. Run it again later with more data.

- ModesQuick roast for a raw idea, full gate before you spend money, post-launch check once you have data

### Position it

Who you serve, why they pick you and how you say it.
Agents 02 to 05

02Talk to Customers
An interview guide, a plan for ten conversations and a summary of what you heard, with every claim graded on evidence.

- ServicesTrigger-moment research and Blair Enns's diagnose-first method
- SoftwareThe Mom Test and Teresa Torres's Continuous Discovery Habits
- ProductBob Moesta's switch interview

03Your Customer
An ICP with the trigger moment, the buying unit and an evidence grade on every claim.

- ServicesJobs to be done and trigger-moment mapping
- SoftwareApril Dunford's best-fit customer derivation
- ProductBob Moesta's Four Forces of Progress

04Positioning
Your competitive alternatives, what's different, the value that enables, who cares most and your market category.

- ServicesDavid C. Baker and Blair Enns on expertise positioning
- SoftwareApril Dunford's Obviously Awesome and Anthony Pierri
- ProductMarty Neumeier, Al Ries and Jack Trout
- LocalCategory, geography and trust
- MediaBeat, point of view and format

05Messaging
A messaging house with one core message and three proof-backed pillars, plus your one-liner, pitch, headlines and answers to the top objections.

- ServicesThe expertise claim from Baker and Enns, and Donald Miller's StoryBrand
- SoftwareAnthony Pierri's headline formula and Emma Stratton's Make It Punchy
- ProductCopyhackers voice-of-customer research

### Package it

What you sell, what it costs and whether the numbers work.
Agents 06 to 08

06Your Offer
Your offer in one paragraph: what's included, for whom, how it's packaged and the guarantee.

- All modelsThe Value Proposition Canvas
- ServicesAlex Hormozi's Grand Slam Offer
- SoftwareMadhavan Ramanujam's leaders, fillers and killers
- ProductMark Joyner's The Irresistible Offer

07Pricing
The value metric, the pricing model, your price points and the anchor, backed by willingness-to-pay research.

- ServicesBlair Enns's Pricing Creativity and Alan Weiss on value-based fees
- SoftwareMadhavan Ramanujam's Monetizing Innovation
- ProductDan Ariely on anchoring and William Poundstone's Priceless

08The Numbers
The five metrics for your model, a 12-month model and a verdict on whether the economics work at your price.

- All modelsLean Analytics' One Metric That Matters, unit economics (CAC, LTV, payback, contribution margin), bottom-up TAM and break-even

### Audience

Attention and leads before you need them.
Agents 09 and 10

09Founder Content
Content pillars, a point of view, the right platform, a cadence you can keep up and a plan to reuse every piece.

- ServicesDavid C. Baker's advice to publish the thinking you'd sell
- SoftwareAndy Raskin's strategic narrative
- ProductFounder story and distinctive brand assets
- MediaAn editorial system

10Lead Magnet
One lead magnet with its promise, format, the segment it captures and the bridge to your paid offer.

- ServicesAn audit or diagnostic
- SoftwareA free tool
- ProductA quiz
- LocalA first-visit offer
- MediaA content upgrade

### Launch it

The page, the launch, the first customers and keeping them.
Agents 11 to 15

11Landing Page
A section-by-section page spec with the copy, ordered for one conversion goal and scored for clarity, relevance, value and anxiety.

- ServicesStoryBrand, or problem-agitate-solve long form
- SoftwareFletch and Anthony Pierri's homepage frameworks
- ProductEugene Schwartz's awareness levels
- All modelsPeep Laja's page scoring

12Launch
A pre-launch, launch and post-launch plan with your warm list, the assets and a day-by-day calendar.

- ServicesThe founding-client offer
- SoftwareDesign partners, then beta, then launch week
- ProductJeff Walker's Product Launch Formula or the drop model
- LocalSoft opening, then grand opening
- MarketplacesSupply first

13Get Customers
Three channels to test, one to focus on, the numbers that decide and your weekly routine.

- All modelsThe Bullseye framework from Traction and Brian Balfour's channel-model fit
- ServicesDaniel Priestley's Key Person of Influence
- SoftwareBalfour's Four Fits, Predictable Revenue or growth loops
- ProductPaid acquisition unit economics
- MarketplacesSolving the cold-start problem

14Convert
Your path from lead to paid: discovery call, proposal and follow-up, or funnel, checkout and lifecycle emails.

- ServicesBlair Enns's Win Without Pitching
- SoftwareSPIN Selling, Sandler and Great Demo! for sales-led; activation for product-led
- ProductBaymard checkout research and lifecycle flows
- LocalThe CLOSER sales framework
- MediaSponsor sales

15Retain
A client's first 90 days after they say yes: the activation milestone, onboarding, the engagement loop and when to ask for renewal or referrals.

- ServicesKickoff to a quick win within 30 days
- SoftwareActivation and net revenue retention
- ProductPost-purchase flows, RFM segmentation and Nir Eyal's Hook model
- LocalRebooking at checkout

FAQ

## Questions, answered

What do I need to run it?

Claude, in the app or Claude Code. Each agent installs as a Claude skill. You add them once and run them in your own account, so your business details stay with you.

How is this different from a set of prompts?

Each agent is a full workflow with its own questions, a version for each business model and an output template. They share one context file, so later agents use what earlier ones produced.

Do I have to run the agents in order?

No. Run the setup step first, then start wherever the pressure is. The recommended sequence starts with the Go / No-Go, and you're free to skip around.

What if my business doesn't fit one model neatly?

The setup step picks the closest model and notes the hybrid, for example services with a digital product on the side. Each agent uses the main model and flags where the second one changes the advice.

What if I want help using it?

The Read gives you my written diagnosis of what the agents produced. The Build is the same system with me 1:1 for three months. Compare the options →

Startup GTM advisor · a fractional CMO alternative for founders from 0 to $1M

# You've built the product. Now build the go-to-market that gets you to $1M.

1:1 go-to-market advisory for founders who need CMO-level thinking before a full-time CMO makes sense: positioning, ICP, pricing, demand and a repeatable path to revenue. You work every week with an operator who scaled startups from zero to $10M.

Find what's capping your revenue → See what's included ↓    Madalena Rugeroni · ex-Google, advisor and investor · scaled startups from 0 to $10M in revenue · runs a portfolio of internet businesses today     Madalena RugeroniFounder of Madgrowth, Mazo and Favorite People

Advising founders at startups like

Sound familiar?

## The product is working. Revenue isn't keeping up.

Between zero and $1M, go-to-market rarely has a full-time owner. It sits with the founder, on top of everything else.

01

### Positioning is fuzzy

Customers like the product but can't explain what it does. Every deal needs you in the room.

02

### Pricing was a guess

You picked a number to get started. It's now leaving money on the table or slowing deals down.

03

### Growth depends on you

Most customers came from your network or your own outreach. Nobody else on the team could run the motion.

04

### Lots of channels, little traction

Some LinkedIn, some outbound, a launch, an agency trial. Plenty of activity and no channel that compounds.

How it works

## Weekly go-to-market work with an experienced operator

01

### A 15-minute call

Where you are, what's stuck and whether I'm the right person to help. If I'm not, I'll tell you.

02

### GTM diagnosis

In our first session we go through positioning, ICP, pricing, channels and numbers, and pick the one constraint holding revenue back.

03

### Working sessions

Up to four a month on what's live: a pricing change, an outbound sequence, a launch, your first GTM hire.

04

### Chat in between

Unlimited. Send the deck, the landing page or the cold email before it goes out.

What's included

Fractional CMO, consultant or advisor?

## Four ways to get senior go-to-market help before $1M

A fractional CMO joins your team part-time and runs marketing. A GTM consultant delivers a project and leaves. A GTM advisor works with you every week while your team does the work. Here's how they compare.

|  | What you get | Typical cost | Best when
| Full-time CMO | A senior leader who owns marketing and builds the team | A full executive salary, plus months of hiring | You have a proven motion and budget to scale it
| Fractional CMO | A part-time CMO inside the team, usually a few days a month | £4,800 to £7,200 a month for four days in the UK (Primewise, 2026) | You need someone to run marketing and manage people
| GTM consultant | A defined project: a positioning sprint, a pricing study, a launch plan | A fixed project fee | You know the one problem and want it solved once
| Startup GTM Advisory | Weekly working sessions, unlimited chat and reviews before things ship. Your team executes | 3,000€ a month, 3-month minimum | You own go-to-market as a founder and want to find what's capping revenue

Who it's for

## Built for founders between 0 and $1M

### A good fit if…

- You have a product and your first customers
- You own go-to-market yourself and haven't hired a senior GTM lead
- Any model: B2B, B2C, marketplace, SaaS or otherwise
- You want someone to think with, and your team ships between sessions

### Not a fit if…

- You're pre-product and still deciding what to build. Start here instead
- You want an agency to run campaigns for you
- You're past $1M with a GTM team in place

FAQ

## Questions, answered

Are you a fractional CMO?

I work as your go-to-market advisor, which sits one step before a fractional CMO. A fractional CMO usually joins the team a few days a month and runs marketing. I work with you every week on positioning, pricing, ICP and channels, review what your team builds, and your team does the execution. When you're ready for a fractional or full-time CMO, we define the role together.

How much does a fractional CMO cost compared with this?

A 2026 benchmark of 53 UK fractional CMOs by Primewise puts a four-day-a-month retainer at £4,800 to £7,200 a month. Startup GTM Advisory is 3,000€ a month with a 3-month minimum, for up to four working sessions plus unlimited chat. It suits founders who need senior thinking and have a team that ships.

Do you take one-off go-to-market consulting projects?

No. The work is monthly, because go-to-market changes need a few cycles to test and adjust. The 3-month minimum covers finding what's capping revenue, changing it and seeing whether the change worked.

Do you only work with SaaS startups?

No. I work with B2B, B2C, marketplace and services-led startups, because the go-to-market fundamentals carry across. B2B SaaS founders also get Mazo for the work between sessions.

Is this hands-on execution?

It's advisory. We make the decisions together and I review what your team builds before it ships. If you need someone to run campaigns, an agency is a better fit.

How is this different from hiring a Head of Growth?

A senior GTM hire takes months to find and costs a full salary. This can start after a 15-minute call, and when you're ready to hire, we define the role together.

Is there a minimum commitment?

Three months. That's enough time to find what's capping revenue, change it and see whether the change worked. After that it's month to month.

Why only five founders?

So each founder works with someone who knows their numbers, their customers and what we decided last session.

What happens on the call?

15 minutes on where you are, what's stuck and whether this is the right help. You'll leave with the first thing to fix, whether or not we work together.

I'm not running a startup yet. I want to start something.

Then the main Madgrowth path fits better: work out what to sell, who it's for and what to charge →

Title: The 5 Builder Archetypes: which business fits you · Madgrowth

The Builder Diagnostic

# The five Builder Archetypes

A Builder Archetype describes how you're wired to build a business: where your leverage comes from, how much risk you take and who you sell to. It tells you which businesses will fit you before you spend a year on the wrong one.

The short answer
- There are five Builder Archetypes: The Broadcaster, The Advisor, The Productizer, The Venture Builder and The Orchestrator.
- They come from the free Builder Diagnostic by Madgrowth, built for leaders in tech with 5 to 10+ years of experience.
- Each archetype is a position on five dimensions: Engine, Bet, Tempo, Moat and Buyers.
- Most people are a blend, so the diagnostic gives you a primary and a secondary archetype.

### The Broadcaster

Your name is the distribution. You build in public, and demand comes to you.

### The Advisor

A few clients who pay properly for judgment that took a decade to build.

### The Productizer

Package once, sell many times. You turn what you know into things that work without you.

### The Venture Builder

The long game. You'd rather spend two years building something that could be worth twenty.

### The Orchestrator

You build the machine that does the work: teams, systems and leverage.

## Which business fits each archetype?

| Archetype | Businesses that fit
| The Broadcaster | Newsletters and media brands, cohort programs, audience-first launches and digital products
| The Advisor | Fractional leadership, high-ticket consulting, advisory retainers and fixed-price audits
| The Productizer | Toolkits and templates, self-serve courses and productized services with a fixed scope and price
| The Venture Builder | SaaS and micro-SaaS, AI tools that replace a workflow, and industry marketplaces
| The Orchestrator | Boutique agencies and studios, AI-assisted service delivery and done-for-you offers

## The five dimensions behind the archetypes

The diagnostic places you on five dimensions. Neither end is better. They describe where you get leverage and what kind of business will feel natural to run.

| Dimension | One end | The other end
| Engine | You | The machine
| Bet | Reversible | All-in
| Tempo | Long game | This week
| Moat | What you know | Who knows you
| Buyers | A handful | Thousands
- Engine: whether the business runs on you (your name, your judgment) or on a machine (a team, a system, software).
- Bet: whether you prefer reversible steps with evidence first, or going all-in when you believe in something.
- Tempo: whether you play long games that compound, or work in weekly sprints.
- Moat: whether people pay for what you know, or come to you because of who knows you.
- Buyers: whether you want a handful of high-trust clients, or thousands of customers.

## Why your archetype matters before you pick a business

Senior operators rarely fail for lack of skill. They fail by picking a model that fights how they work: an Advisor launching a low-ticket course that needs thousands of buyers, or a Venture Builder stuck in a services business capped by their calendar. Knowing your archetype first narrows the options to the ones you'll actually keep running.

If you're still deciding between models, read fractional, consulting or software: which business to start.

## Questions people ask

What are the Builder Archetypes?

The Builder Archetypes are five profiles from the Madgrowth Builder Diagnostic that describe how someone is wired to build a business: The Broadcaster, The Advisor, The Productizer, The Venture Builder and The Orchestrator. Each one points to the business models that fit how that person works.

Who created the Builder Archetypes?

Madalena Rugeroni created the Builder Archetypes and the Builder Diagnostic for Madgrowth, for leaders in tech deciding between a fractional role, a services business or software.

How is a Builder Archetype calculated?

The diagnostic asks short work scenarios and scores the answers on five dimensions: Engine, Bet, Tempo, Moat and Buyers. Your scores are matched to the closest archetype profile, and the second closest becomes your secondary archetype.

Is the Builder Diagnostic free?

Yes. It takes about three minutes. You see your archetype on the page, and you can get the full profile and the free Expertise Audit by email.

Builder Archetype

# The Broadcaster

Your name is the distribution. You build in public, and demand comes to you.

Definition
The Broadcaster is one of the five Builder Archetypes in the Madgrowth Builder Diagnostic. It describes people best suited to creator-led businesses where your voice is the distribution: newsletters and media brands, cohort programs, audience-first launches and digital products.

## How The Broadcaster works

When you say what everyone else is thinking, the right people show up in your inbox. Attention is your raw material, and unlike most operators, you enjoy the exposure.

The businesses that fit you are the ones where your voice is part of the product: audience-first launches, media-style brands and digital offers with demand in place before the product exists. Get visible first, then build the machine behind it.

## What your full profile adds

If the diagnostic places you here, your full profile goes further: the specific businesses built for The Broadcaster, the ones that fight this wiring, the blind spot that stalls most people with this archetype, and how you work at your best and under stress. It also shows your secondary archetype, because most people are a blend.

Title: The Advisor Builder Archetype: businesses that fit · Madgrowth

Builder Archetype

# The Advisor

A few clients who pay properly for judgment that took a decade to build.

Definition
The Advisor is one of the five Builder Archetypes in the Madgrowth Builder Diagnostic. It describes people best suited to high-ticket businesses that sell senior judgment to a few clients: fractional leadership, high-ticket consulting, advisory retainers and fixed-price audits.

## How The Advisor works

You're wired for depth: fewer people, harder problems, more trust. When a genuinely ambiguous call needs making, you're the calmest person in the room and the one they call back. That trait is an asset, and most operators never learn to price it.

The businesses that fit you sell judgment: fractional leadership, high-ticket consulting with a sharp named offer, advisory retainers or a paid teardown at a fixed price. Fifteen people with budget who know exactly what you fix is enough.

## What your full profile adds

If the diagnostic places you here, your full profile goes further: the specific businesses built for The Advisor, the ones that fight this wiring, the blind spot that stalls most people with this archetype, and how you work at your best and under stress. It also shows your secondary archetype, because most people are a blend.

Title: The Productizer: Builder Archetype · Madgrowth

Builder Archetype

# The Productizer

Package once, sell many times. You turn what you know into things that work without you.

Definition
The Productizer is one of the five Builder Archetypes in the Madgrowth Builder Diagnostic. It describes people best suited to packaged, repeatable offers sold many times: toolkits and templates, self-serve courses and productized services with a fixed scope and price.

## How The Productizer works

You're wired to ship. While others are still naming the planning doc, you have a v1 in someone's hands. Your instinct is to turn messy, bespoke work into something with edges: a template, a system, a fixed price. That instinct is most of the job.

The businesses that fit you are packaged and repeatable: toolkits and templates people buy off the shelf, self-serve courses with no delivery time and productized services with a fixed scope and price. Revenue should grow with copies sold, and you already sense that.

## What your full profile adds

If the diagnostic places you here, your full profile goes further: the specific businesses built for The Productizer, the ones that fight this wiring, the blind spot that stalls most people with this archetype, and how you work at your best and under stress. It also shows your secondary archetype, because most people are a blend.

Title: The Venture Builder: Builder Archetype · Madgrowth

Builder Archetype

# The Venture Builder

The long game. You'd rather spend two years building something that could be worth twenty.

Definition
The Venture Builder is one of the five Builder Archetypes in the Madgrowth Builder Diagnostic. It describes people best suited to owned software and long-game product bets: SaaS and micro-SaaS, AI tools that replace a workflow, and industry marketplaces.

## How The Venture Builder works

You're wired to build the machine itself. Where others see a service to sell, you see a workflow to automate, a product to own and upside your calendar can't cap. You're also willing to bet big on it, and that mix of patience and conviction is rare.

The businesses that fit you are owned systems: SaaS or micro-SaaS in a niche you know well, AI tools that replace a workflow you've run a hundred times, and software where the build itself is the moat. Your industry knowledge is an advantage most technical founders lack.

## What your full profile adds

If the diagnostic places you here, your full profile goes further: the specific businesses built for The Venture Builder, the ones that fight this wiring, the blind spot that stalls most people with this archetype, and how you work at your best and under stress. It also shows your secondary archetype, because most people are a blend.

Title: The Orchestrator: Builder Archetype · Madgrowth

Builder Archetype

# The Orchestrator

You build the machine that does the work: teams, systems and leverage.

Definition
The Orchestrator is one of the five Builder Archetypes in the Madgrowth Builder Diagnostic. It describes people best suited to service businesses run on systems and teams instead of your hours: boutique agencies and studios, AI-assisted service delivery and done-for-you offers.

## How The Orchestrator works

You're wired to run things. Your talent is delivery: the system that makes quality reliably repeatable and keeps running in the weeks you're away. You get your leverage from orchestrating the work, and you're comfortable handing the doing to others.

The businesses that fit you are machines with margins: a boutique agency or studio with a small senior team, AI-assisted service delivery that runs your playbook, and done-for-you offers where the system is the product. You can scale past your own calendar faster than any other archetype.

## What your full profile adds

If the diagnostic places you here, your full profile goes further: the specific businesses built for The Orchestrator, the ones that fight this wiring, the blind spot that stalls most people with this archetype, and how you work at your best and under stress. Title: Claude skills for business: position, price, launch · Madgrowth

Claude skills

# Claude skills for business: position, price and launch an offer

Claude is only as good as the method you give it. These are fifteen AI agents, plus a free one, that install as Claude skills and take you from idea to launch: whether to build it, who buys, how you're positioned, what you sell, what it costs and how you launch. Each one asks about your business first and hands you a finished document.

Madalena Rugeroni · Founder of Madgrowth · ex-Google · Updated 18 September 2026

The short answer
- Claude skills are folders of instructions that Claude loads when a request matches them, so it runs the same method every time.
- They work in Claude Code (as folders) and in the Claude app (uploaded as a zip under Customize > Skills), on every Claude plan with code execution turned on.
- The Stack by Madgrowth is 15 AI agents that install as Claude skills, plus the free Expertise Audit, covering go/no-go, customers, positioning, offer, pricing, content, launch, acquisition, conversion and retention.
- Each agent reads one shared context file and uses the version for your business model: services, software, product, local, media or marketplaces.

## What are Claude skills?

A Claude skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file that tells Claude how to do one job and when to do it. According to Anthropic's Agent Skills documentation, Claude keeps only each skill's name and description in mind, at roughly 100 tokens per skill, and reads the full instructions when your request matches. That means you can install a whole library and Claude only opens the skill it needs.

For business work, that consistency is the whole point. A prompt depends on what you remember to paste at eleven at night. A skill asks the same questions and follows the same method every time, so the tenth run is as good as the first.

## Which Claude skills does a business need?

A business needs skills for the decisions that are expensive to get wrong: whether to build it, who the customer is, how you're positioned, what you sell, what you charge and how you get the first customers. I put Go / No-Go before anything that looks like marketing, because a beautiful launch plan for the wrong idea is still the wrong idea. These are the agents in The Stack, each installed as a Claude skill, in the order I'd run them.

### Start here

| Agent | # | What it produces
| Expertise Audit | Free | Your three strongest angles from the career you already have: who buys, the problem in their words and your proof.
| Start | Setup | A context file every other agent reads: business model, stage, sales motion, price band, team, geography and build capacity.

### Decide

| Agent | # | What it produces
| Go / No-Go | 01 | A go, no-go or not-yet verdict on your idea, scored against your Builder Archetype, with the assumption that decides it, the cheapest test and a pre-mortem.

### Position it

| Agent | # | What it produces
| Talk to Customers | 02 | An interview guide, a plan for ten conversations and a summary of what you heard, with every claim graded on evidence.
| Your Customer | 03 | An ICP with the trigger moment, the buying unit and an evidence grade on every claim.
| Positioning | 04 | Your competitive alternatives, what's different, the value that enables, who cares most and your market category.
| Messaging | 05 | A messaging house with one core message and three proof-backed pillars, plus your one-liner, pitch, headlines and objection answers.

### Package it

| Agent | # | What it produces
| Your Offer | 06 | Your offer in one paragraph: what's included, for whom, how it's packaged and the guarantee.
| Pricing | 07 | The value metric, the pricing model, your price points and the anchor, backed by willingness-to-pay research.
| The Numbers | 08 | The five metrics for your model, a 12-month model and a verdict on whether the economics work at your price.

### Audience

| Agent | # | What it produces
| Founder Content | 09 | Content pillars, a point of view, the right platform, a cadence you can keep up and a plan to reuse every piece.
| Lead Magnet | 10 | One lead magnet with its promise, format, the segment it captures and the bridge to your paid offer.

### Launch it

| Agent | # | What it produces
| Landing Page | 11 | A section-by-section page spec with the copy, ordered for one conversion goal.
| Launch | 12 | A pre-launch, launch and post-launch plan with your warm list, the assets and a day-by-day calendar.
| Get Customers | 13 | Three channels to test, one to focus on, the numbers that decide and your weekly routine.
| Convert | 14 | Your path from lead to paid: discovery call, proposal and follow-up, or funnel, checkout and lifecycle emails.
| Retain | 15 | A client's first 90 days after they say yes: onboarding, the engagement loop and when to ask for renewal or referrals.
Every agent credits the frameworks it uses, like April Dunford on positioning, Blair Enns and Madhavan Ramanujam on pricing and Bob Moesta on customer interviews. The full list of methods per business model is on The Stack page.

## How are these agents different from a folder of prompts?

They work as one system. A setup step classifies your business once, writes it to a context file and every other agent reads it. Later agents also read what earlier ones produced, so pricing knows your ICP and the landing page knows your messaging.

- A method per business model. A fractional CMO pricing a retainer and a SaaS founder pricing a plan need different methods. Each agent loads the one for your model.
- Questions before answers. Each agent asks for what's missing before it writes, so the output is about your business and not a plausible guess.
- A document at the end. An ICP, an offer, a price, a launch calendar. Files you keep and edit.

## How do you install Claude skills?

| Where | How to install | How to run
| Claude Code | Put each skill folder in ~/.claude/skills/ for all projects, or .claude/skills/ in one project | Ask naturally, or type /skill-name
| Claude app | Turn on code execution in Settings, then upload each skill as a zip under Customize > Skills and switch it on | Ask naturally. Claude picks the skill that matches
Skills don't sync between Claude Code and the app, so install them wherever you work. Sources: the Claude Code skills docs and the Claude help center. If you'd like to write your own, read how to create a Claude skill, with a working SKILL.md example.

## Are third-party Claude skills safe?

Treat a skill like software you install: if you didn't write it and can't read it, don't run it. Anthropic's documentation warns that a skill can direct Claude to run tools or code in ways that don't match its stated purpose. The Madgrowth agents are Markdown instructions and reference files, with no scripts and nothing that fetches content from the internet, so you can read every line before you install them.

## Questions people ask

What are Claude skills?

Claude skills are folders of instructions, and optionally reference files and scripts, that Claude loads when a request matches the skill's description. They let Claude follow the same method every time for a specific job, like writing positioning or pricing an offer, without pasting a prompt.

Are Claude skills free to use?

The Claude help center lists skills as available on Free, Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise plans, with code execution turned on. Some skills are free to download and others are sold, like The Stack. The free Expertise Audit comes by email with the Madgrowth Builder Diagnostic.

What are the best Claude skills for business?

The ones that end in a document you would actually use on Monday: a positioning statement, a price, an offer, a launch plan. Look for skills that ask about your business before writing, follow a named method and change the advice for your business model.

Do Claude skills work in Claude Code and the Claude app?

Yes. In Claude Code, skills are folders in ~/.claude/skills/ or a project's .claude/skills/. In the Claude app, you upload a zip under Customize > Skills. Skills don't sync between the two, so install them in each place you use them.

Is Madgrowth affiliated with Anthropic?

No. Madgrowth is an independent business run by Madalena Rugeroni. The skills are built to run in Claude, which is made by Anthropic.

Guides

# Guides for leaders in tech building a business of their own

Plain answers to the questions that stop experienced operators: what to sell, which business to build, and how to launch it, whether that's software, an audience, an agency, digital products or a fractional practice.

Madalena Rugeroni · Founder of Madgrowth · ex-Google

### What to sell after leaving a tech job

Sell an outcome you've delivered more than once to a buyer who already pays for it. How to find your angle after a tech job, test it and avoid the traps.

### Fractional, consulting or software: which business should you start after tech?

Fractional and consulting work pay within weeks; software pays later but grows past your hours. How ex tech leaders choose, with a side-by-side comparison.

### How to build a micro SaaS from your tech career

Build a micro SaaS from a workflow you know: validate with pre-sales, price it for B2B and win your first 10 customers. Ideas, AI MVPs and real timelines.

### How to build an audience business from your expertise

Build an audience business: pick a narrow beat from your career, one platform and a weekly cadence, then sell services or products before subscriptions.

### How to start an agency after a career in tech

To start an agency, pick one client type and outcome, sell a productized offer first, price for margin and hand delivery to a small senior team and systems.

### How to sell digital products from your expertise

Sell digital products by choosing a format your buyer already pays for, pre-selling it, then doing the distribution. Formats, pricing and platforms compared.

### How to become a fractional executive

Become a fractional executive by packaging one problem you've solved as a monthly role with set days and outcomes, then selling it to your network first.

### How to price fractional and consulting services

Price fractional services from the cost of the problem and the hire it replaces. Day rate vs retainer vs value pricing, with European day rates in euros.

URL: https://www.madgrowth.io/guides/what-to-sell-after-tech/
Title: What to sell after leaving a tech job · Madgrowth

Guide

# What to sell after leaving a tech job

Madalena Rugeroni · Founder of Madgrowth · ex-Google · Updated 18 September 2026 · 9 min read

The thing to sell after leaving a tech job is an outcome you've delivered more than once, to a buyer who already spends money to get it. Put it in one sentence: who buys, what problem, your proof. Then test that sentence with 10 real buyers. The website and the product can wait.

The short answer
- An angle is one sentence: a specific buyer, their problem, and your proof that you've fixed it before.
- Look for outcomes you've delivered three times, problems people already bring you, and whoever held the budget for them.
- One angle can become a fractional role, advisory, a productized service or software. Pick the shape that fits how you like to work.
- Test it cheaply: name 20 companies, have 10 conversations about what they did last time, then ask for a small paid project.
- The three traps: selling your job title, a buyer too broad to see themselves, and buyers who feel the pain with no budget.

## What can you sell after leaving a tech job?

You can sell four things: part of your week in a leadership seat, your judgment, a fixed package of work, or a product. Each one is a different business, with different income and a very different week.

A fractional executive takes a real role at one or more companies, part time (fractional CMO, VP engineering, head of growth), usually on a monthly retainer. An advisor or consultant sells judgment on one specific problem, by project or retainer. A productized service is a fixed scope at a fixed price, like an audit or a four-week sprint.

Software and digital products (tools, templates, courses, paid newsletters) sell without your hours attached. They also take the longest to earn anything.

All four run on the same raw material: an outcome someone will pay for. My rule is outcome first, format second. I run both kinds myself. Madgrowth sells advice and AI agents, and Mazo is software I built. The format question has its own guide: fractional, consulting or software.

## How do you find your niche from the career you already have?

Your niche sits where three things overlap: work you've done repeatedly, problems people already ask you about, and buyers who had budget for that result. David C. Baker makes this case in The Business of Expertise. Expertise comes from seeing the same problem many times, and a narrow focus is how you see it often enough to beat a generalist.

So start with an honest inventory of the last 5 to 10 years. Be strict. Your CV will flatter you.

### Step 1: list the outcomes you've owned more than once

Write down results you were accountable for, across different companies or teams. Built the first sales team. Moved a product from sales-led to self-serve. Cut infrastructure costs before a fundraise. Took a company into Germany. Rebuilt an onboarding flow that was losing users.

My bar is three times. By the third, you know which parts change from company to company and which stay the same, and that pattern is what a client pays for.

Put a number on everything you can: pipeline, revenue, cost, time, headcount. "Grew pipeline from 2M€ to 8M€ in 18 months at a Series B fintech" (an illustrative example) is a line a buyer can believe. A job title on its own proves very little.

### Step 2: write down what people already ask you about

Go through the last year of messages, coffee requests and calls from former colleagues. Note what they wanted help with: hiring a first engineer, pricing a new plan, fixing a stalled launch, deciding whether to raise.

This list is worth more than it looks, because the problem arrives already worded by someone who has it. Copy their words exactly. They'll end up in your offer.

### Step 3: find who paid for that outcome

For each outcome, ask who signed off on the money when it mattered. Alan Weiss calls this person the economic buyer: whoever owns the budget for the problem. It's often someone other than the person who feels it most. A marketing manager lives with a flat pipeline. The CEO of a 40-person company approves the spend to fix it.

Then check whether this kind of company has paid an agency, a consultant or a contractor for it before. If yes, a budget line already exists and you're competing for it. That's good news.

If nobody in your target group has ever paid for outside help here, you're asking them to invent a new line item. I wouldn't start there. It's a much harder sale.

### Step 4: write the angle as one sentence

Put the three pieces together: a specific buyer in a specific moment, the problem in their words, and your proof. For example: "Seed-stage B2B founders who've just raised and have nobody owning pipeline. I've built that function from zero three times." If you can't fill in all three parts, what you have is a topic, and nobody buys a topic.

## What does a good angle look like?

A good angle names a buyer you could list 20 companies for, a moment that makes the problem urgent, and proof with numbers in it. The moment is the part people skip.

Companies buy outside help right after something changes: a funding round, a new VP, a missed quarter, a market launch, a board deadline. Tie your angle to one of those and the buyer knows exactly when to call you.

Here's what that looks like next to a plain title. These are illustrative profiles, not real clients.

| Career (illustrative) | What people write | Angle: buyer, problem, proof | Where I'd start
| Head of growth at two B2B SaaS scale-ups | "Fractional growth lead" | Series A SaaS founders whose paid acquisition stalled after the round. Rebuilt the channel mix at two companies. | Fractional retainer, 1 to 2 days a week
| Engineering director at three startups | "Tech consultant" | CTOs at 30 to 80-person companies facing their first security certification because a big customer asked for it. Led it three times. | Productized readiness sprint at a fixed price
| VP product at a sales-led company that added self-serve | "Product advisor" | Founders adding a self-serve plan who need pricing and onboarding redesigned. Ran that transition twice. | Advisory project, then a monthly retainer
| RevOps director | "RevOps expert" | Heads of sales at 50 to 200-person companies moving to a new CRM before the next financial year. Ran four migrations. | Fixed-scope migration, later a software tool
The titles in the second column leave the buyer guessing what happens in month one. The angles describe a situation the buyer is in right now, and that's what gets a reply.

## Which kind of business should your angle become?

Pick the shape by how you want to work, because one angle can support several. The pipeline angle above could be a fractional seat, a fixed-price audit, a course for first-time growth hires or a reporting tool. What changes is how your week looks and how much of your time each euro costs.

I group these preferences into five Builder Archetypes:

- Broadcaster: your name is the distribution. Content, courses, community and paid newsletters.
- Advisor: a few clients who pay properly for judgment. Fractional seats and advisory retainers. More on the Advisor archetype.
- Productizer: package the work once and sell it many times. Audits, sprints, templates.
- Venture Builder: the long game. Software or a company that could be worth far more than your hours.
- Orchestrator: you build the team or system that delivers the work. Agencies and studios.
Your refusals narrow it fastest. If you won't be on camera or post publicly, drop the audience businesses. If you don't want client calls most days, services will wear you down. If you won't build software and have no technical partner, software can wait.

Time matters too. An audit can fit around a full-time job. A fractional seat needs at least a day a week, and a founder who needs you on a Tuesday afternoon. If fractional is where you're heading, read how to go fractional next.

## How do you test the angle before you quit your job?

Test it with named buyers, conversations about the past and a small paid offer, before you spend a cent on a brand, a site or a product. All of it fits into a few weeks of evenings next to a job.

### Name 20 companies

Write down 20 real companies that fit the buyer in your sentence, plus the name of the person who'd approve the spend. If you can't get to 20, the angle is too vague to act on or the market you can reach is too small. Both are worth knowing now.

### Have 10 conversations about what already happened

Ask people how they handled this problem the last time it came up: what they tried, who they hired, what it cost and who decided. Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test is the short book I'd read first. Its core idea is simple. Ask about past behaviour and people tell you the truth. Ask about your idea and they're polite.

Leave your pitch out of these calls. Listen for their words, past spend, and whether the problem is on this quarter's list.

### Ask for money with a small fixed offer

Once a few conversations confirm the problem, offer something small with a clear scope and a price. Say, a two-week pipeline diagnostic for 2,500€ that ends in a written plan. A yes gives you revenue and a reference.

"Let's talk next quarter" means the urgency isn't there yet, however warm the call felt. For the number itself, see how to price fractional and consulting work.

### Read the evidence honestly

Keep going if people describe the problem before you do, they've paid for outside help on it before, and at least one person agrees to pay. Change the angle if you get lots of interest and no budget, every call turns into free advice, or buyers can't say when they'd need you.

One practical point if you're still employed: read your contract for clauses on outside work, conflicts of interest and intellectual property before you take paid work.

## What mistakes should you avoid when choosing what to sell?

The first one to check is selling your job title. A title tells the buyer which seat you sat in and nothing about what changes for them. The rest are close relatives of that one.

- Selling the title. "Fractional CMO" is a category buyers understand, and that helps. On its own, it gives nobody a reason to pick you over the next profile. Attach the focus: fractional CMO for B2B SaaS companies entering the DACH market.
- Too broad. "I help B2B companies grow" covers almost everyone, so nobody sees themselves in it. If a buyer can't tell within one sentence that you mean them, they move on.
- Buyers with no budget. Pre-revenue founders, employees paying out of their own pocket, and your old team (rather than their boss) all feel the pain. Few of them can sign a retainer.
- Picking the most interesting angle over the one with proof. Start with what you can prove. Move towards the fun one once clients trust you.
- Building before selling. Months on a platform, a brand or a course before a single buyer conversation. The test above takes weeks and costs almost nothing.
- Pricing from your last salary. Dividing your old salary into a day rate ignores the time you'll spend selling, the weeks between clients, and what the problem costs the client.

## Should you pick one angle or keep your options open?

Pick one angle for the next 90 days and park the rest on a list. Each angle needs its own buyer list, its own message and its own conversations. Test three at once and you end up with too little evidence on any of them.

Committing is less final than it feels. A narrow position is easy to widen once people refer you. A vague one is hard to sharpen later, because nobody remembers what you do. April Dunford makes a related point in Obviously Awesome: start from the customers who get the most value from you, and describe yourself in terms they already understand.

The order I'd follow: write three candidate angles, rank them by strength of proof and how easily the buyer can pay, and test the top one. If the evidence is weak after 10 conversations, move to number two.

If you want help getting to those three, the free Expertise Audit skill comes with the Builder Diagnostic. It runs in Claude, asks about the work you've done, and gives you your three strongest angles, each with the buyer, the problem and your proof.

## Find your angle and the business shape that suits you

The Builder Diagnostic takes about 3 minutes and shows which of the five Builder Archetypes fits how you like to work. You also get the Expertise Audit skill by email, to find the three strongest angles in your own career. When you've picked one and want to position, package and price it, The Stack takes you through it.
Run the free Builder Diagnostic

## Questions people ask

Can I start a consulting business while still employed in tech?

Yes, if your contract allows it. Read the clauses on outside work, conflicts of interest and intellectual property before you take paid work. I'd start with a small fixed-scope offer like an audit. It fits around a full-time job far more easily than a weekly fractional seat.

What if my experience feels too generic to find a niche?

Start with outcomes. List results you delivered more than once, each with a number, a context and the moment a company needed it: after a round, a new VP, a missed quarter. Where a repeated outcome meets a buyer with budget, your niche is narrower than your CV suggests.

Should I niche by industry or by function?

Pick whichever gives you stronger proof and a buyer list you can actually name. A function (pricing, RevOps, security certification) travels across industries. An industry focus (fintech, healthtech) makes referrals easier. My favourite is one of each, like RevOps for fintech scale-ups. That's the sharpest angle you can have.

What is the difference between a fractional executive and a consultant?

A fractional executive holds an ongoing leadership role part time, owns results and usually manages people or budget, on a monthly retainer. A consultant or advisor comes in for a specific problem or project and hands over recommendations or a plan. You can start with one and add the other later.

How do I know if anyone will pay for my expertise?

Ask the people you want to sell to how they solved the problem last time and what they spent. If they've paid an agency, a contractor or a consultant before, a budget exists. Then offer a small paid project at a fixed price. A yes is the strongest evidence you'll get.

URL: https://www.madgrowth.io/guides/how-to-go-fractional/
Title: How to become a fractional executive · Madgrowth

Guide

# How to become a fractional executive

Madalena Rugeroni · Founder of Madgrowth · ex-Google · Updated 18 September 2026 · 10 min read

To become a fractional executive, pick one leadership problem you've solved more than once. Package it as a monthly role with a set number of days and named outcomes. Then sell it to companies that need that leader before they can justify a full-time hire. Your first two or three clients should come from people who already know your work. And start alongside your job only if your contract and your employer's interests allow it.

The short answer
- Fractional means an ongoing leadership role (CMO, CTO, CPO, VP or head of a function), usually one or two days a week, for a monthly fee.
- Startups and scale-ups hire you after a round, a leader leaving or a board asking for a plan, before they can afford a full-time executive.
- Your offer states the days per month, the outcomes you own, a minimum term of three months or more, and your client cap.
- First clients come from people who've seen your work. Find the ones whose companies are in a trigger moment and ask about that problem.
- Skip fractional if you want to advise without owning results, or want income that grows past your own hours.

## What does fractional mean, and how is it different from interim, consulting or advising?

Fractional means you hold a real leadership role inside a company for part of the week. You have the title, you own the function's results, and often you have a team. You sit in the leadership meetings, set the plan and answer for the number, on one or two days a week instead of five. The company pays you a monthly retainer.

Buyers mix it up with three other models. Two questions separate them: how much of your time the company gets, and who owns the result.

| Model | What you're hired for | Time | Who owns the result | How it's usually priced
| Fractional executive | Running a function the company can't staff with a full-time leader yet | A set share of the week, ongoing | You, inside the company | Monthly retainer
| Interim manager | Covering a gap: a leader left, a turnaround, a merger | Full-time for a fixed period | You, for the length of the contract | Day rate
| Consultant | A defined project with a clear output | Whatever the project needs | You own the output, the client owns putting it in place | Fixed project fee
| Advisor | Judgment on call for the founder or leadership team | A few hours a month | The team, who decide and do the work | Monthly access fee, sometimes equity
Ownership is where I draw the line. If the company expects you to own pipeline, the roadmap or the engineering team, you're fractional, whatever the contract says. If they expect you to tell them what you'd do, you're an advisor. Price and scope it that way.

On titles: buyers search for "fractional CMO" or "fractional CTO", so use the title they recognise. Then name the problem you fix. "Fractional CMO" covers brand work for a consumer app and pipeline for B2B SaaS, and those are two different jobs. I've been Country Manager at Too Good To Go and Global Head of Growth at Amplemarket, and I would never sell those as the same role.

## Who hires a fractional CMO, CTO or CPO?

Founders and CEOs hire fractional leaders when the company has outgrown what the founding team can do in a function, and can't yet justify, afford or attract a full-time executive for it. In tech, that's usually a startup or scale-up with some revenue and a function nobody senior owns. Outside tech, it's often an established small or mid-sized business that needs a technology or product leader for the first time.

What makes them buy now is a trigger. "We should probably get someone" has never signed a retainer. Something has to change:

- A funding round closed and investors expect a plan for the money.
- A head of marketing, product or engineering left and the gap is showing.
- A quarter was missed and the board wants to know who owns the fix.
- The company is about to hire its first full-time executive for the function and doesn't know what good looks like.
The person who signs is usually the CEO or founder. They own the budget, and they feel the gap most. So write the trigger in their words. "We raised in March and nobody owns pipeline" is a sentence a founder actually says. Nobody asks for "end-to-end growth enablement".

They'll compare you with a full-time hire, which means months of recruiting and the risk of picking the wrong person. At their stage, your offer has to look better than that.

## What should you package as a fractional executive?

Package a fixed monthly scope: one problem, a set number of days, the outcomes you own in the first 90 days, a minimum term and a cap on how many companies you take on.

### Start from a problem you've solved more than once

I'd only build an offer on something you've done at least twice, at a company whose stage is close to the buyer's. Say, taking sales from founder-led to the first five reps, or setting up product management somewhere that never had it. If you're unsure which is strongest, start with working out what to sell from your tech career before you write any scope.

### Write the outcomes first, then the activities

Alex Hormozi's offer thinking works well here. Start from the result the buyer wants, list everything that could stop them getting it, and make your scope the set of things that removes those obstacles.

For a fractional role, that gives you outcomes like "a hiring plan and the first two hires made" or "a pipeline report the board trusts". Weekly calls and Slack access are delivery details. They go further down the page.

### Set the days and the boundaries

Say the time plainly: one day a week, two days a week, or a number of days a month. Then write the boundaries that protect those days: which meetings you attend, how fast you reply between days, what's out of scope. Skip this and a one-day role quietly becomes three days at the same fee.

### Add a minimum term and an exit

Three months is the shortest term I'd accept for a leadership role, because the first month is mostly learning the company. After that, go monthly with a notice period. Also write down how the role ends well. The cleanest ending is handing over to the full-time leader you helped hire.

An illustrative example, all together:

- Role: fractional head of growth for B2B SaaS companies that raised a seed round in the last six months.
- Time: 2 days a week, with replies within one working day in between.
- Outcomes in 90 days: one acquisition channel tested with clear numbers, a weekly pipeline report, and a job description plus shortlist for the first marketing hire.
- Term: 3-month minimum, then monthly with 30 days' notice.
- Capacity: two companies at a time.

## How much should you charge as a fractional leader?

Charge a monthly retainer tied to the days and outcomes in your scope. Then check it against two numbers: what the company would pay for a full-time hire, and what you need to earn across the clients you can realistically hold.

Don't show an hourly rate. The moment you do, the client starts counting hours instead of results.

Public benchmarks for fractional fees in Europe are thin, and many come from platforms selling fractional services. So I look at interim management, which has better data. The German interim management association DDIM projects an average interim day rate of 1,317€ for 2026 in its DDIM Marktstudie 2026, averaged across functions and seniority levels. It's a German figure for interim work, so use it as a sanity check on what a senior day costs a company in that market.

Now the maths. Say you sell 2 days a week to each client, roughly 8 days a month, and price the retainer at the equivalent of 1,000€ a day. That's 8,000€ a month per client. Two clients take four days of your week and bring in 16,000€ a month before tax and costs, with one day left for selling and admin.

A third client doesn't fit. If that ceiling is below what you need, raise the price or change the shape of the offer.

Blair Enns and Alan Weiss both argue for pricing against the value of the result. Fractional work suits that well, because the buyer has a clear alternative cost. The full method is in how to price fractional and consulting work. For comparison, my own go-to-market advisory for startups is 3,000€ a month with up to four sessions and a three-month minimum. That's an advisory shape, with less time and less operating ownership than a fractional role.

## How do you get your first fractional clients?

Your first two or three fractional clients come from people who've already seen you work, like former managers and ex-colleagues who now run companies or teams. Trust comes faster with them, and a retainer runs on trust.

### 1. Write the list

Open a spreadsheet and write down everyone who's seen your work closely enough to describe it. Aim for 50 names. Add their company and whether they could buy or refer.

### 2. Mark who is near a trigger

Go through the list against the triggers above: who just raised, lost a leader or opened a job for the role you'd fill. Investors see these moments early, across many companies, so give them their own conversation.

### 3. Send a short, specific message

Name the problem and the stage, and ask one question. For example: "I'm starting to work as a fractional head of growth for seed-stage B2B companies, two days a week, for teams where nobody owns pipeline yet. Is anyone in your portfolio in that spot right now?" A message like that is easy to forward, which is exactly what you want.

### 4. Make the first call about their problem

Ask what happens if the problem isn't fixed in six months, and what they've already tried. Bob Moesta's jobs-to-be-done interviews are a good model: you want the story of what changed and why now.

If they need more certainty before a retainer, offer a short paid diagnostic with a fixed fee that turns into the first month if they continue.

### 5. Publish what you know, once a week

While those conversations run, write one post a week about the problem you fix: a mistake you've seen, or a decision you'd now make differently. It gives your list something to forward and lets people outside your network find you.

Fractional marketplaces help once your offer is clear. They take a cut, though, so I'd keep them as a second channel.

## Can you do fractional work while you're still employed?

Yes, if your contract allows it, there's no conflict of interest with your employer, and you have the hours to do the role properly. Check all three before you send the first message.

In the EU, Directive (EU) 2019/1152 (Article 9) says employers can't prohibit workers from taking up employment with other employers outside their work schedule, or treat them badly for it. It's written about employment, so self-employed side work may be treated differently. The same article lets member states allow restrictions on objective grounds, including business confidentiality and avoiding conflicts of interest.

Each country applies this differently, and your contract may still include exclusivity, intellectual property or non-solicitation clauses. This is general information, not legal advice. Read your contract, and if anything is unclear, pay an employment lawyer in your country for an hour.

In practice, three rules keep you out of trouble:

- Don't work for your employer's competitors, customers or suppliers.
- Don't use company time, company equipment or anything you learned in confidence.
- Don't approach colleagues or clients from your current job.
Time is the harder constraint. A two-day fractional role doesn't fit next to a full-time job, however much you want it to. What fits is a smaller shape: an advisory retainer of a few hours a month, or a fixed-scope diagnostic delivered over a few weekends.

Use those to test the buyer and the price. When one or two clients want a full fractional scope, you have a reason and a date to leave.

## When is fractional the wrong fit?

Fractional is the wrong fit if you don't want to own a function's results week to week, or if you want income that grows past your own calendar. Be honest about this now. Months spent building a pipeline for a role you'll resent is an expensive way to find out.

- You like the thinking and dislike operating. Fractional means running a team inside someone else's company, politics included. If you enjoy the hard call more than the weekly operating, I'd go for an advisory retainer. The Advisor archetype describes this profile: fewer clients, higher fees for judgment, and a strong habit of undercharging.
- You want to build something that runs without you. Fractional income is capped by your days. If you'd rather design how the work gets delivered and hire people to do it, look at a small senior agency or studio. That's the Orchestrator archetype.
- You want to own a product. If software could solve the problem you keep solving, compare the two paths properly in fractional, consulting or software before you commit.
- You don't want to keep selling. Good fractional roles end when the company hires a full-time leader. That means your pipeline never gets to stop.

## Check whether fractional suits how you work

The free Builder Diagnostic takes about 3 minutes. It shows your Builder Archetype and which business models fit it, fractional roles included. If you already have a draft offer and want my written view before you take it to your network, that's The Read.
Run the Builder Diagnostic

## Questions people ask

How many clients can a fractional executive take on at once?

Count the days first. If each client gets one or two days a week, two or three clients is the practical limit, because you still need time every week to sell and do admin. Put the cap in your offer so clients know it from day one.

Do I need to set up a company to work as a fractional executive in Europe?

Not always. In many European countries you can start as a self-employed sole trader and set up a company later, once the income justifies the extra cost and admin. Tax, VAT and social security rules differ by country, so talk to a local accountant before you send your first invoice.

Can I be a fractional CTO or CMO if I never held that exact title?

Yes, if you've owned the outcomes the role covers, like running the engineering team or owning pipeline, at a company close to the buyer's stage. Buyers check whether you've fixed their problem before. Put that problem and your proof in the offer, and use the title they search for.

What should I do if a fractional client asks me to join full-time?

Decide your answer before it happens, because it comes up when a role goes well. If it's a no, offer to help recruit and hand over to the full-time leader. That's one of the best ways to end a fractional role. If it might be a yes, agree the terms openly and give your other clients proper notice.

Should I join a fractional marketplace to find my first clients?

Start with your network. Those people have already seen your work, so trust comes faster. Marketplaces help once you can say exactly what you sell and to whom. They take a cut of each client and expect you to pitch yourself, so I'd keep them as a second channel.
